analysis.one_liner: Diverts part of Social Security payroll taxes into personal retirement accounts and slows guaranteed benefit growth.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate in November 2003 with zero cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let most workers born after 1949 divert a slice of their Social Security payroll taxes into personal retirement accounts invested like federal employees' Thrift Savings Plan funds, administered by the government or, once a balance reached $10,000, by certified investment firms, insurance companies, or credit unions. In exchange, guaranteed benefits would grow more slowly for people who did not pay an extra tax to keep them, and workers earning under $30,000 would get a new minimum benefit plus matching deposits into their accounts. It would also cut transfers to the Medicare trust fund and create a commission to recommend eliminating federal programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers would gain a new guaranteed minimum Social Security benefit (120% of the poverty line, phased in 2007-2011) and a matching deposit of up to $500 a year into their account, including a portion of their Earned Income Tax Credit if they chose. Workers with accounts would own assets that could be inherited, unlike traditional benefits. Financial institutions certified to hold accounts would gain a new stream of payroll-funded assets.

how_it_helps.text: Creates federally administered personal retirement accounts for everyone born after 1949, funded by redirecting 4% of the first $32,500 of wages from the Social Security trust fund, with investment options modeled on the Thrift Savings Plan [S2][S3].
Establishes a new minimum monthly Social Security benefit equal to 120% of the poverty line for low earners who stay in the traditional benefit track, phased in from 2007 to 2011 [S3].

Provides workers earning under $30,000 a matching deposit of $100 plus 50% of designated wages or Earned Income Tax Credit amounts, up to $500 a year, credited only into their personal retirement account [S3].

Requires account funds to carry no sales loads and to charge fees as a single stated annual percentage of assets, and allows account balances over $10,000 to be moved to privately administered accounts at certified institutions [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Retirees who do not pay an extra tax would see guaranteed benefits grow with prices instead of wages, a growing cut over a working life, and their traditional benefit would be reduced by the value diverted into their account. Account investments would be at the holder's own risk, with no government guarantee. The Social Security trust fund would lose revenue during the transition, offset in part by reduced transfers to the Medicare trust fund and by a commission empowered to recommend eliminating federal programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Future retirees and Medicare's trust fund

drawbacks.text: For new retirees who keep the basic benefit track, initial benefits would be indexed to inflation rather than wage growth, so guarantees would shrink relative to wages every year a person works [S3].
The traditional benefit would be reduced by the actuarial value of the amounts diverted into a worker's account, so the account replaces guaranteed benefits rather than adding to them [S3].
Account holders would sign an acknowledgment that investments are made at their own risk and that neither the government nor the trustee guarantees a return or protects against loss [S3].
Workers who made no election by age 26 would be deemed to have chosen an account, making the private-account structure the default rather than the opt-in choice [S3].

The bill would reduce transfers to the Medicare trust fund to help finance the transition and would create a nine-member commission to recommend realignment or elimination of federal agencies and programs [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill traded real gains for the lowest earners — a poverty-level benefit floor and matching deposits — against a structural benefit cut for everyone else, because price indexing plus the account offset would leave middle-class retirees with substantially smaller guaranteed checks than current law. The accounts would carry genuine market risk with no government backstop, and the transition would strain both the Social Security and Medicare trust funds. Whether the accounts made retirees better off would depend entirely on market returns over a lifetime.

outcome.mechanism: Lindsey Graham introduced it in November 2003 with no cosponsors; the Senate Finance Committee never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on November 18, 2003, by Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina [S1][S5].
The Senate's only actions were to read it twice and refer it to the Committee on Finance, where no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded before the Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in committee, Social Security's guaranteed benefit formula was left untouched and financial firms did not gain the new payroll-funded account channel; at the same time, the bill's proposed minimum benefit and matching deposits for low-wage workers never materialized either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Defenders of the traditional Social Security structure

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and no senator cosponsored the bill, so the record shows only a single Republican sponsor with no measurable support from either party.

industries.note: The bill would route a percentage of every worker's payroll into investment accounts, creating a large new pool of assets, and would let balances over $10,000 move to privately managed accounts at certified firms. Fund managers would profit from managing this money, though the bill barred sales loads and required fees to be stated as one annual percentage of assets, limiting the skim.

Both were named as eligible certified institutions that could hold privately administered personal retirement accounts, gaining new fee-paying account holders. The bill barred sales loads and capped fee structures, so their gains would come from scale rather than high charges.
